questions.q: What is a survivorship rule, as defined in this lesson?
options: The documented logic that decides which source's value wins for a specific attribute when building a golden record
A rule that determines how long a database backup is retained
A rule for deciding which employees survive a company reorganization
A security policy for encrypting master data
questions.explain: Survivorship rules are specifically about which source's value is chosen for each attribute when reconciling matched records into a golden record.

questions.q: Which survivorship strategy would most sensibly apply to a phone number that changes over time?
options: Most recent wins — the value from whichever source last updated the field
Oldest value always wins, regardless of updates
The value is permanently frozen at the time the record was created
A coin flip determines the winning value
questions.explain: The lesson specifically gives 'most recent wins' as sensible for attributes like phone numbers or emails that change over time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'the CRM always wins' is usually the wrong way to define survivorship for an entire record?
options: Because CRMs are never accurate for any field
Because a single source is often reliable for some attributes (like contact info) but unreliable for others (like billing address), so rules need to be defined per attribute
Because CRMs do not store customer data
Because it is illegal to designate a trusted source
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a source's reliability varies by attribute — strong for the fields it's actively maintained for, weak for fields it rarely touches — so a blanket global rule breaks down.

questions.q: What does the 'most complete wins' survivorship strategy do?
options: It always picks the longest text value regardless of accuracy
When one source has a populated (non-null) value and another is blank, the populated value wins by default
It deletes any field that is not fully populated
It requires every source to have an identical value before proceeding
questions.explain: Most complete wins is described as a simple, often-necessary rule: a non-null value beats a blank one when no stronger rule applies.

questions.q: Per this lesson, where should survivorship rules be documented?
options: Nowhere — they should be left as informal institutional knowledge
In the written MDM policy from Lesson 5, per attribute and per domain, with a named owner who can approve changes
Only in a single engineer's personal notes
In a customer-facing marketing document
questions.explain: The lesson ties survivorship documentation back to the written MDM policy introduced in Lesson 5, warning that undocumented logic buried in code is fragile and unauditable.
